analysis.subject: earth-science
analysis.pageCoverage: Covers the numeric geologic time scale, how radioactivity enabled age assignment, definitions of atoms and isotopes, half-life, four radiometric parent to daughter series, measurement error, and linking isotopic mineral dates with fossil relative ages to set boundaries.

overview.headline: Radioactive decay provides numeric ages for the geologic time scale

keyPoints.point: The assignment of rock ages in thousands, millions, and billions of years was made possible by the discovery of radioactivity
keyPoints.quote: The assignment of ages of rocks in thousands, millions, and billions of years was made possible by the discovery of radioactivity.

keyPoints.point: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time for one-half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms
keyPoints.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

keyPoints.point: four parent/daughter decay series are especially useful for dating and include carbon to nitrogen and potassium to argon
keyPoints.quote: four parent/daughter decay series are especially useful: carbon to nitrogen, potassium to argon, rubidium to strontium, and uranium to lead.

keyPoints.point: Isotopic techniques are used to measure the time at which a particular mineral within a rock was formed
keyPoints.quote: Isotopic techniques are used to measure the time at which a particular mineral within a rock was formed.

keyTerms.gloss: discovery that enabled assignment of numeric ages in thousands of years to rocks
keyTerms.quote: The assignment of ages of rocks in thousands, millions, and billions of years was made possible by the discovery of radioactivity.

keyTerms.gloss: length of time required for one half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms
keyTerms.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

keyTerms.gloss: radioactive form of an element with different number of neutrons but same protons
keyTerms.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

keyTerms.gloss: basic unit of each chemical element containing a nucleus with protons and neutrons
keyTerms.quote: The basic unit of each chemical element is the atom.

keyTerms.gloss: methods used to measure time of mineral formation within a rock
keyTerms.quote: Isotopic techniques are used to measure the time at which a particular mineral within a rock was formed.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Teaches the constant-rate half-life definition that underlies numeric age calculations from parent and daughter counts.
componentPlan.focusQuote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Reinforces memorable numeric facts about Earth and fossils and the stated limits on measurement accuracy.
componentPlan.focusQuote: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old?

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Groups the four parent to daughter systems the page identifies as especially useful for dating geologic materials.
componentPlan.focusQuote: four parent/daughter decay series are especially useful: carbon to nitrogen, potassium to argon, rubidium to strontium, and uranium to lead.
